// Deterministic parser for the authored LR explanation markdown files
// (PT<NNN>-explanations.md). Pure: given a file's text it returns structured
// records. It never invents a tag, a percentage, or any prose — anything it
// cannot read verbatim becomes a skip with a reason.
//
// Recognised shapes (all present in the PT101-PT140 corpus):
//   ## S<n> · Q<n> — <question type>
//   > no explanation given                     -> unexplained question
//   ### Stimulus / ### Prompt
//   ### Written (single style)                 -> one explanation, style "single"
//   ### Written (Standard|Brief|Another Way)   -> three explanations
//   ### Standard | ### Brief | ### Another Way -> three explanations (alt spelling)
//   ### Answer-choice notes (no authored breakdown)
//   ### Answer-choice tags (no authored prose)
//   ### Answer choices                         -> unexplained question's choices
//
// Choice line:
//   **A. <text>** — <tag> (<N>% of students)
//   **A. <text>** (<N>% of students)           -> tag stays null

const QUESTION_SPLIT = /^## (?=S\d+ \u00B7 Q)/m;
const HEADING_RE = /^S(\d+)\s\u00B7\sQ(\d+)\s\u2014\s(.+)$/;
// v2 corpus states the correct letter explicitly, straight from LSAT Lab's
// `correctanswer` field. It is authoritative; the choice tag is not.
const CORRECT_ANSWER_RE = /^\*\*Correct answer:\*\*\s*([A-E])\s*$/m;
const CHOICE_RE =
  /^\*\*([A-E])\.\s+([\s\S]*?)\*\*(?:\s+\u2014\s+([\s\S]+?))?\s+\((\d+)% of students\)\s*$/;
const STEP_RE = /^-\s+\*\*(.+?):\*\*\s*([\s\S]*)$/;

const STYLE_HEADINGS = new Map([
  ['Written (single style)', 'single'],
  ['Written', 'single'],
  ['Written (per-choice only)', 'single'],
  ['Written (Standard)', 'standard'],
  ['Written (Brief)', 'brief'],
  ['Written (Another Way)', 'another_way'],
  ['Standard', 'standard'],
  ['Brief', 'brief'],
  ['Another Way', 'another_way'],
  ['Answer-choice notes (no authored breakdown)', 'single'],
  ['Answer-choice tags (no authored prose)', 'single'],
  // Some files split the one explanation across two sections: the breakdown
  // under its own heading and the per-choice prose under "Answer choices".
  ['Argument breakdown', 'single'],
  ['Answer choices', null], // choices only; prose (if any) merges into "single"
]);


// Two kinds of structural markup can trail a question block and leak into the
// last answer choice's prose. Both are punctuation between questions, never
// content, and dropping them here covers every consumer at once because all of
// them read the lines this function emits.
//
//   1. A bare thematic break ("---"), which separates every question block.
//   2. A section heading ("# Section 4 (Logical Reasoning)"). Questions are
//      split on "##" headings, so a single-hash section heading is not a
//      boundary and stays attached to the question that precedes it. This hit
//      the last question of every section.
const THEMATIC_BREAK_RE = /^\s*(-{3,}|\*{3,}|_{3,})\s*$/;
// Matched narrowly on purpose. A bare /^#\s/ also catches authored content —
// "# of important issues" and "# that are Wilson" are shorthand for "number
// of", not headings — and treating those as a section boundary silently drops
// a question's answer choices. Every real heading in the corpus is one of
// "# Section N (...)" or "# PrepTest N ...".
const STRUCTURAL_HEADING_RE = /^#{1,2}\s+(Section|PrepTest)\b/;

// Neither rule may fire inside a fenced code block. Authored explanations draw
// inference bars there ("-------------------" under two premises), which is
// content, not punctuation, and stripping it silently mangles the proof.
const FENCE_RE = /^\s*(```|~~~)/;

function splitSubsections(body) {
  const out = [];
  let current = null;
  let inFence = false;
  for (const line of body.split('\n')) {
    if (FENCE_RE.test(line)) inFence = !inFence;
    // A section heading ends this question. Anything after it — the heading, a
    // trailing "> Note:" about the next section, further separators — belongs
    // to what follows, not to the choice whose prose we are still collecting.
    if (!inFence && STRUCTURAL_HEADING_RE.test(line)) break;
    const m = inFence ? null : /^###\s+(.+?)\s*$/.exec(line);
    if (m) {
      current = { heading: m[1], lines: [] };
      out.push(current);
    } else if (current) {
      if (!inFence && THEMATIC_BREAK_RE.test(line)) continue;
      current.lines.push(line);
    }
  }
  return out;
}

function parseChoiceBlock(lines) {
  const choices = [];
  let current = null;
  // A choice header may wrap across lines when the tag is a dual label, e.g.
  //   **A. text** — Bad Conclusion Match
  //   Bad Validity Match (2% of students)
  // so we buffer from the "**X. " opener until the percentage terminator.
  let header = null;
  for (const raw of lines) {
    const line = raw.trimEnd();
    if (/^\*\*Answer choices\*\*\s*$/.test(line)) continue;

    if (header !== null) {
      header = `${header}\n${line}`;
    } else if (/^\*\*[A-E]\.\s/.test(line)) {
      header = line;
    }

    if (header !== null) {
      const m = CHOICE_RE.exec(header);
      if (m) {
        current = {
          letter: m[1],
          text: m[2].trim(),
          tag: m[3] ? m[3].trim() : null,
          percent: Number(m[4]),
          prose: [],
        };
        choices.push(current);
        header = null;
      } else if (header.split('\n').length > 6) {
        header = null; // not a choice header after all; drop the buffer
      }
      continue;
    }

    if (!current) continue;
    if (line.trim() === '') {
      if (current.prose.length) current.prose.push('');
      continue;
    }
    current.prose.push(line);
  }
  return choices.map((c) => ({
    ...c,
    prose: c.prose.join('\n').trim() || null,
  }));
}

function parseBreakdown(lines) {
  const steps = [];
  let inBreakdown = false;
  // Which layout this breakdown uses, fixed by its first step. Italic labels
  // are only steps in an italic-layout breakdown; in a bold-layout one they
  // are cues inside a step ("*rephrase:*", "*Given that*").
  let layout = null;
  for (const raw of lines) {
    const line = raw.trimEnd();
    if (/^\*\*Argument breakdown\*\*\s*$/.test(line)) {
      inBreakdown = true;
      continue;
    }
    if (/^\*\*Answer choices\*\*\s*$/.test(line)) break;
    const m = STEP_RE.exec(line);
    if (m && (inBreakdown || true)) {
      inBreakdown = true;
      layout ??= 'bold';
      steps.push({ label: m[1].trim(), text: m[2].trim() });
      continue;
    }
    // Alternate authored shape: the label is its own bold line, with the step
    // text in the paragraph(s) below it (e.g. "**Given that ...**").
    const h = /^\*\*(.+?)\*\*\s*$/.exec(line);
    if (h) {
      inBreakdown = true;
      layout ??= 'bold';
      steps.push({ label: h[1].replace(/\s*\.\.\.\s*$/, '').trim(), text: '' });
      continue;
    }
    // Italic-label shape (PT154): "*Evaluate:* text" opens a step inline, and
    // a bare "*Rhett's Claims*" line opens one whose text is the list below.
    // Only inside the breakdown and only in the italic layout.
    const italicOk = inBreakdown && layout !== 'bold';
    const it = italicOk && /^\*([^*]+?):\*\s*(.*)$/.exec(line);
    if (it) {
      layout = 'italic';
      steps.push({ label: it[1].trim(), text: it[2].trim() });
      continue;
    }
    const ih = italicOk && /^\*([^*]+)\*\s*$/.exec(line);
    if (ih) {
      layout = 'italic';
      steps.push({ label: ih[1].trim(), text: '' });
      continue;
    }
    if (!inBreakdown) continue;
    if (line.trim() && steps.length) {
      const prev = steps[steps.length - 1];
      prev.text = prev.text ? `${prev.text}\n${line}` : line;
    }
  }
  return steps.filter((s) => s.text.trim());
}

/** Parse one PT<NNN>-explanations.md file. */
export function parseExplanationFile(text, fileName) {
  const preptestMatch = /^#\s+PrepTest\s+(\d+)/m.exec(text);
  if (!preptestMatch) throw new Error(`${fileName}: no "# PrepTest <n>" header`);
  const preptest = Number(preptestMatch[1]);

  const questions = [];
  const skipped = [];

  for (const chunk of text.split(QUESTION_SPLIT).slice(1)) {
    const [headingLine, ...rest] = chunk.split('\n');
    const body = rest.join('\n');
    const hm = HEADING_RE.exec(headingLine.trim());
    if (!hm) {
      skipped.push({ id: `PT${preptest} ${headingLine.trim()}`, reason: 'unparseable question heading' });
      continue;
    }
    const section = Number(hm[1]);
    const questionNumber = Number(hm[2]);
    const qid = `PT${preptest}-S${section}-Q${questionNumber}`;
    const questionType = hm[3].trim();

    const noteMatch = /^>\s+(.*)$/m.exec(body);
    const sourceNote = noteMatch ? noteMatch[1].trim() : null;
    const unexplained = /^>\s+no explanation given\s*$/im.test(body);

    const subs = splitSubsections(body);
    const stimulus = subs.find((s) => s.heading === 'Stimulus');
    const prompt = subs.find((s) => s.heading === 'Prompt');
    const styleSections = subs.filter((s) => STYLE_HEADINGS.has(s.heading));
    const stated = CORRECT_ANSWER_RE.exec(body);

    // Video-only questions. LSAT Lab publishes no written explanation for
    // these, so the corpus records the correct letter and a note and nothing
    // else — there is no stimulus, prompt, or choice text in the source to
    // transcribe. Carry them as real questions with a known answer and
    // is_explained false rather than dropping them: a question that exists
    // with no explanation is truer than a question that does not exist.
    //
    // Gated on the whole empty signature (no stimulus AND no prompt AND no
    // style section) plus an explicit correct answer, so a partially
    // malformed question — a stimulus but no prompt, say — still surfaces as
    // a skip instead of being silently downgraded to a stub.
    if (!stimulus && !prompt && !styleSections.length) {
      if (!stated) {
        skipped.push({ id: qid, reason: 'no question content and no "**Correct answer:**" line' });
        continue;
      }
      questions.push({
        preptest,
        section,
        questionNumber,
        qid,
        questionType,
        stimulus: null,
        prompt: null,
        sourceNote,
        isExplained: false,
        correctChoice: stated[1],
        choices: [],
        explanations: [],
      });
      continue;
    }

    if (!stimulus || !prompt) {
      skipped.push({ id: qid, reason: 'missing Stimulus or Prompt section' });
      continue;
    }

    if (!styleSections.length) {
      skipped.push({ id: qid, reason: 'no recognised answer-choice / explanation section' });
      continue;
    }

    // Choices are repeated under every style, but some questions print them
    // only once (after the last style), so take the first block that is whole.
    const choiceBlocks = styleSections.map((s) => parseChoiceBlock(s.lines));
    const choices = choiceBlocks.find((b) => b.length >= 5) ?? choiceBlocks[0] ?? [];
    if (choices.length < 5) {
      skipped.push({ id: qid, reason: `only ${choices.length} answer choices parsed (need 5)` });
      continue;
    }
    // Correctness comes from the authored "**Correct answer:** X" line, which
    // is LSAT Lab's own `correctanswer` field. Choice tags are NOT reliable:
    // some correct choices carry no tag, others carry a descriptive one
    // ("Conclusion", "Weakens"). Only when the line is absent (older corpus
    // files) do we fall back to a tag reading "Correct".
    let correctChoice = null;
    if (stated) {
      correctChoice = stated[1];
      if (!choices.some((c) => c.letter === correctChoice)) {
        skipped.push({ id: qid, reason: `stated correct answer ${correctChoice} is not among the parsed choices` });
        continue;
      }
    } else {
      const tagged = choices.filter((c) => c.tag && /^Correct\b/i.test(c.tag));
      if (tagged.length === 1) {
        correctChoice = tagged[0].letter;
      } else if (!unexplained) {
        skipped.push({
          id: qid,
          reason:
            tagged.length === 0
              ? 'no "**Correct answer:**" line and no choice tagged "Correct"'
              : `no "**Correct answer:**" line and ${tagged.length} choices tagged "Correct"`,
        });
        continue;
      }
    }
    const pctSum = choices.reduce((a, c) => a + c.percent, 0);
    if (pctSum < 95 || pctSum > 105) {
      skipped.push({ id: qid, reason: `percentages sum to ${pctSum} (outside 95-105)` });
      continue;
    }


    const byStyle = new Map();
    const hasSingle = styleSections.some((s) => STYLE_HEADINGS.get(s.heading) === 'single');
    for (const sec of styleSections) {
      // "### Answer choices" carries no style of its own; when the file also
      // has a breakdown section, its per-choice prose belongs to that one.
      const style = STYLE_HEADINGS.get(sec.heading) ?? (hasSingle ? 'single' : null);
      if (!style) continue;
      const styleChoices = parseChoiceBlock(sec.lines);
      const steps = parseBreakdown(sec.lines);
      const choiceProse = styleChoices
        .filter((c) => c.prose)
        .map((c) => ({ letter: c.letter, prose: c.prose }));
      if (!steps.length && !choiceProse.length) continue;
      const existing = byStyle.get(style);
      if (existing) {
        existing.steps.push(...steps);
        for (const n of choiceProse) {
          if (!existing.choiceProse.some((p) => p.letter === n.letter)) existing.choiceProse.push(n);
        }
      } else {
        byStyle.set(style, { style, steps, choiceProse });
      }
    }
    const explanations = [...byStyle.values()];


    questions.push({
      preptest,
      section,
      questionNumber,
      qid,
      questionType,
      stimulus: stimulus.lines.join('\n').trim(),
      prompt: prompt.lines.join('\n').trim(),
      sourceNote,
      isExplained: !unexplained && explanations.length > 0,
      correctChoice,
      choices: choices.map(({ prose, ...c }) => ({ ...c, isCorrect: c.letter === correctChoice })),
      explanations,
    });

  }

  return { preptest, questions, skipped };
}

# Section 1 (Logical Reasoning)

## S1 · Q1 — Paradox

> Note: LSAT Lab offers only a single authored written explanation for this question (no Standard / Brief / Another Way selector).

### Stimulus
Police chief: This department's officers are, of course, prohibited from drinking on the job. However, there is one exception: it is extremely valuable for officers to work undercover to investigate nightclubs that have chronic crime problems, and officers may drink in moderation during such work.

### Prompt
Which one of the following, if true, most helps to justify the exception to the police department's rule stated above?

### Written (single style)
**Argument breakdown**
- **Given that ...:** Cops are usually prohibited from drinking on the job.
- **Why is it that ...:** Cops are allowed to drink in moderation during work if they're working undercover in nightclubs?
- **Evaluate / Goal:** This one seems to play off common sense, so we can probably predict the answer.

Why are cops allowed to drink if they're working undercover in a nightclub? Because they're supposed to be blending in with all the normal people there, most of whom are drinking.

Let's look for that, or any other reason why cops working undercover in a nightclub are allowed to have a couple drinks.

**Answer choices**
**A. Only very experienced police officers are allowed to work undercover investigating nightclubs.** — Unclear Impact (2% of students)
This provides a distinction about undercover work in nightclubs — it's going to be a very experienced cop.

Okay, does that explain why we let them drink? Is there a common sense connection like, "If you're a very experienced cop, you're allowed to drink in moderation?"

No, even very experienced cops should presumably be as sober as possible.

**B. Many nightclub patrons would suspect that people in a nightclub who refrained from drinking were police officers.** — Correct (93% of students)
This explains why undercover cops are allowed to drink in the nightclub. They don't want to blow their cover by being the only square who isn't drinking.

Other patrons at the nightclub would be like, "Hey, Eddie, why are you drinking water? What are you, some sort of Narc?"

**C. Over the last several years, the police department has significantly increased its undercover operations in nightclubs.** — No Impact (2% of students)
For this to work, we'd have to think " because the police department has invested a bunch in undercover nightclub operations, they let the undercover cops do a little drinking on the job".

There's no common sense connection there.

**D. Most police officers believe that allowing officers to drink during undercover work in nightclubs does not cause significant problems.** — Too Weak / No Distinction (4% of students)
This helps somewhat, because it makes us see why letting undercover cops drink a little bit on the job probably isn't too bad. Most cops don't think it'll cause significant problems.

But that leaves plenty of room for most cops to think it still causes some tiny problems. And it leaves room for up to 49% of cops to think that drinking on the job causes significant problems.

So it's not a super powerful endorsement. But more importantly, it has nothing to do with "justifying the exception ". We're tasked with solving why undercover work at nightclubs is different from the usual prohibition of drinking on the job.

This answer doesn't say, " Unlike for other settings, when it comes to nightclubs, most cops don't think drinking on the job would cause significant problems". So this answer does nothing to explain why we treat nightclub drinking differently from other on-the-job drinking.

**E. For the most part, the public is aware that police officers are allowed to drink during undercover operations in nightclubs.** — No Impact (0% of students)
Whether the public is aware or not aware that undercover cops can drink at the club, doesn't explain why cops are allowed to drink at the club.

## S1 · Q2 — Agree/Disagree

> Note: LSAT Lab offers only a single authored written explanation for this question (no Standard / Brief / Another Way selector).

### Stimulus
Jake: Companies have recently introduced antibacterial household cleaning products that kill common bacteria on surfaces like countertops and floors. It’s clear that people who want to minimize the amount of bacteria in their homes should use cleaning products that contain antibacterial agents.

Karolinka: But studies also suggest that the use of these antibacterial cleaning products can be harmful, since common bacteria that survive the use of these products will eventually produce strains of bacteria that are resistant to antibiotics. That’s why antibacterial agents should not be used in household cleaning products.

### Prompt
The discussion above indicates that Jake and Karolinka agree with each other that which one of the following is true?

### Written (single style)
**Argument breakdown**
- **Jake Karolinka:** I Companies have recently introduced antibacterial household cleaning products that kill common bacteria on surfaces like counter-tops and floors.

But studies also suggest that the use of these antibacterial cleaning products can be harmful, since common bacteria that survive the use of these products will eventually produce strains of bacteria that are resistant to

It’s clear that That’s why people who want antibacterial agents to minimize the should not be used amount of bacteria in household in their homes cleaning products. should use cleaning products that contain antibacterial agents.
- **Evaluate:** Jake and Karolinka agree that household cleaning agents kill some common bacteria.

**Answer choices**
**A. Household cleaning products with antibacterial agents kill some common bacteria.** — Correct (85% of students)
Jake and Karolinka would both agree with this statement.

**B. Household cleaning products with antibacterial agents remove dirt better than do products lacking those agents.** — Out of Scope (0% of students)
Neither Jake nor Karolinka address how well such cleaning agents remove dirt.

**C. The use of antibacterial agents in household cleaning products can produce antibiotic resistant strains of bacteria.** — Half Scope (0% of students)
Karolinka would agree with this statement, but Jake does not address it.

**D. Common household bacteria are a serious health concern.** — Out of Scope (4% of students)
Neither Jake nor Karolinka address whether common household bacteria are a serious health concern.

**E. People should use household cleaning products with antibacterial agents to clean their homes.** — Agree/Disagree (10% of students)
While Jake would agree with this statement, Karolinka would disagree with it.

## S1 · Q3 — Flaw

> Note: LSAT Lab offers only a single authored written explanation for this question (no Standard / Brief / Another Way selector).

### Stimulus
A study of the dietary habits of a group of people who had recently developed cancer and a group without cancer found that during the previous five years the diets of the two groups' members closely matched each other in the amount of yogurt they contained. Yogurt contains galactose, which is processed in the body by an enzyme. In the people with cancer the levels of this enzyme were too low to process the galactose in the yogurt they were consuming. It can be concluded that galactose in amounts exceeding the body's ability to process it is carcinogenic.

### Prompt
Of the following, which one constitutes the strongest objection to the reasoning in the argument?

### Written (single style)
**Argument breakdown**
- **Conclusion:** If you have more galactose in your body than what the body can process, it is carcinogenic (cancer-causing).
- **Evidence:** In a study, the group of people with cancer had such a low level of a certain enzyme that they couldn't process the galactose in the yogurt they were consuming.
- **Evaluate:** The author is taking one fact she knows that is distinct to the cancer group and then concluding that that factor caused the cancer!

What if we had said, "In the people with cancer, the level of hair loss was much higher than in the non-cancer group. Therefore, losing hair is carcinogenic"? That would be a silly conclusion to reach. Maybe the hair loss is unconnected to the cancer. Maybe it's actually an effect of the cancer (or the chemotherapy treatment received by people who have cancer).

When an author presents a correlation, f.e. "the people who were X were also Y", she is likely to conclude that X causes Y. But we always evaluate causal arguments with the same two-pronged mindset: - Is there any other way to explain this correlation? (maybe Y causes X. Maybe some third factor, Z, is causing both of them) - How plausible is the author's causal storyline? (is there any explanation of how X would cause Y? are there any data points that show when someone stopped having X, they stopped having Y?)

We are trained to react to correlations primarily by thinking, "What if it's Reverse Causality? What if there's some Third Factor that's the real cause that we haven't identified with?"
- **Goal:** Find an answer simply describing the author's illegal move of thinking, "Since all the cancer people had low enzyme, the low enzyme is causing the cancer", or find an answer bringing up one of the alternative explanations the author has failed to consider: "Maybe the cancer led to the low enzyme. Maybe there's some other factor, like a certain gene, that both leads to cancer and leads to low levels of this enzyme."

**Answer choices**
**A. The argument fails to consider whether the dietary habits of everyone in the two groups were the same in all other respects.** — Weak Impact (10% of students)
The author does fail to consider other possible differences in diet. We know they ate the same amount of yogurt, but we don't know how the rest of their diets compare.

Learning about the rest of their diets, however, would only matter if we found something different in their diets that helped us find some other way to explain why the cancer / low enzyme group had cancer or low enzyme.

It's not a strong objection to say to the author, "Hey, author, the dietary habits of every single person in two groups were not identical."

You could have 99% of these people on identical diets, and one person eats 1.5 bananas / day while everyone else is eating 1 banana / day, and that sort of fact would already make it true that "the dietary habits of everyone was not the same in all other respects."

That language is so extreme, that it's not a realistic demand we would make of any study that looked at people over a 5 year period.

**B. The argument neglects to recommend that people with low levels of the enzyme avoid eating yogurt.** — Out of Scope: recommend (1% of students)
The author is only trying to prove that X causes Y. Successfully proving that X causes Y doesn't require that you also advise people against doing X.

Someone can prove that "smoking causes lung cancer" without ever saying "I recommend that people don't smoke", so the lack of a recommendation would never be a flaw in an argument that seeks to prove a causal relationship.

**C. The argument focuses on only one substance that can increase the risk of cancer, when it is well known that there are many such substances.** — Out of Scope: other cancer-causes (7% of students)
The author is only trying to prove that X causes Y. Successfully proving that X causes Y doesn't require that you also mention everything else that causes Y.

Someone can prove that "smoking causes lung cancer" without ever saying "working in a coal mine also causes lung cancer". When we're making objections, we're saying "you failed to prove your conclusion", not "there are other things you should have also talked about beyond what your conclusion was saying".

**D. The argument overlooks the possibility that cancer causes low levels of the enzyme.** — Correct (81% of students)
This is your classic Reverse Causality answer. The author presents a correlation: being in the cancer group was correlated with having low levels of the enzyme. Then the author assumes that low enzyme caused the cancer. What if cancer caused the low enzyme?

Having a cancer or other illness can certainly affect your physiology in ways that may throw levels of certain body chemicals out of whack. Maybe the cancer came first and the low enzymes came second.

The most common way to weaken a causal argument is to point out some other way to explain the evidence.

**E. The argument does not specify whether any member of either group lacked the enzyme entirely.** — Irrelevant (1% of students)
We don't care whether anyone had zero enzyme. As long as the enzyme is "low enough" that the person can't process galactose, then the author can make the same argument. It doesn't matter whether that "low enough" is a tiny bit of enzyme, a speck, or nothing at all.

All 26 questions transcribed verbatim from LSAT Lab: stimulus, prompt, answer choices with their tag and student percentage, and the per-choice explanation.

Reformatted 2026-08-03 from the original `## Question N` layout into the corpus-standard `## S2 · Q<n>` layout. No prose was changed; the tag and percentage now sit on the choice line, as everywhere else in the corpus.

PT155 is single-style: only one authored written explanation exists per question.

## S3 · Q3 — Main Conclusion

**Correct answer:** D

### Stimulus
Newspaper columnist: What caused the current recession is a hotly debated question. It is a mistake, however, to assume that answering this question is essential to improving the economy. Corrective lenses, after all, were an effective treatment for myopia long before the cause was known to be genetic.

### Prompt
Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the newspaper columnist's argument?

### Standard
**Argument breakdown**
- **Conclusion:** It's a mistake to assume figuring out what caused the recession is essential to improving the economy.
- **Evidence (after all):** Corrective lenses were an effective treatment for myopia long before the cause was known to be genetic.
- **Evaluate:** Whenever we do Main Conclusion, we read the paragraph differently, because we know that instead of putting the conclusion at the end of the paragraph (the most common place), on Main Conclusion and Role we expect the conclusion to be earlier than (at least some of) the supporting ideas. Specifically, 90% of Main Conclusion questions have a conclusion that is
    - the First Sentence
    - a Rebuttal / Pivot idea

    This one did the second. The first sentence is just a fact. There's no support provided to defend the idea that people are hotly debating what caused the current recession. Then we see that magical however and think, "Is this the conclusion? Am I seeing the ol' Rebuttal / Pivot conclusion formula again?" To clinch our suspicion that this 2nd sentence is the Conclusion, we want to see that it's being Supported. The fact that the 3rd sentence begins with one of the four Support Indicators (FABS = for, after all, because, since) tells us that the 2nd sentence was definitely the conclusion.
- **Goal:** When we have Rebuttal style conclusions, we need to take an extra sec to state our author's position, using the wording of the position she's rebutting. For example, if we hear, "Some people think that ketchup is a vegetable. However, they're wrong", then we need to say that the Conclusion is "Ketchup is not a vegetable". So here the opposing position was that "We need to figure out what caused the current recession in order to improve the economy. It's essential." Our author is saying "No, it's not. That's a mistake. It's not essential. You could improve the economy, even if you didn't figure out what caused the current recession." Let's find the answer that best matches the meaning of the 2nd sentence.

**Answer choices**
**A. Solving a problem never requires finding the root cause of the problem.** — Bad Match (2% of students)
The columnist argues that knowing the cause of the recession is not essential to improving the economy — a narrow claim about one specific situation. This answer says "solving a problem never requires finding the root cause," which is a universal claim that goes far beyond what the columnist asserts. The word "never" transforms a specific observation into an absolute rule. The columnist does not say that finding root causes is never necessary for solving problems; the columnist says it is not essential in this particular case. The myopia analogy supports the possibility that solutions can precede causal understanding, but it does not prove that causal understanding is never needed anywhere. This answer overgeneralizes the conclusion to a degree the argument does not support.

**B. Knowing the cause of the current recession would not necessarily enable people to find a solution to it.** — Necessary vs. Sufficient (20% of students)
This answer confuses "not essential" with "not helpful." The columnist says knowing the cause is not essential — meaning it is not a prerequisite for improving the economy. This answer says knowing the cause would not necessarily enable people to find a solution, which is a claim about whether causal knowledge is sufficient for a solution. These are different logical relationships. The columnist's point is about necessity: you do not need to know the cause to improve things. This answer is about sufficiency: knowing the cause might not be enough to improve things. The columnist is not arguing that knowing the cause would be useless or insufficient; the columnist is arguing that you can make progress without it. The conclusion is about what is not required, not about what might not work.

**C. The question of what caused the current recession is subject to considerable debate.** — Bad Match (1% of students)
This answer restates a piece of background information from the stimulus, not the conclusion. The columnist opens by noting that the cause of the recession is "a hotly debated question" — this sets the stage for the argument but is not the argument's point. The conclusion is the columnist's own assertion that follows: it is a mistake to assume that answering this debated question is essential to improving the economy. Background facts describe the situation; the conclusion tells you what to do about or think about that situation. This answer identifies the scene-setting context rather than the argumentative claim built upon it.

**D. One need not ascertain the cause of the current recession in order to improve the economy.** — Correct (75% of students)
This answer accurately captures the columnist's main conclusion. The argument's structure is: (1) background — the cause of the recession is debated; (2) conclusion — it is a mistake to assume that identifying the cause is essential to improving the economy; (3) evidence — corrective lenses treated myopia effectively before the genetic cause was known. The conclusion, paraphrased, is that one need not ascertain the cause of the recession to improve the economy. This answer matches that claim in scope and content. It does not overstate by claiming causal knowledge is never useful; it does not understate by merely restating the evidence or the background. It captures the core prescriptive insight: improvement can occur without prior identification of the underlying cause.

**E. Long before the cause of myopia was known to be genetic, corrective lenses were being used as an effective treatment for the disease.** — Bad Match (1% of students)
This answer restates the evidence, not the conclusion. The columnist uses the myopia example as an analogy to support the main point: just as myopia was treated before its cause was understood, the economy can be improved without knowing the recession's cause. The fact about corrective lenses is the supporting analogy — it serves the conclusion rather than being the conclusion itself. In argument structure, evidence supports the conclusion; the conclusion is what the evidence is offered to prove. The myopia example is marshaled to prove the columnist's broader point about the recession, making it evidence, not the main conclusion. Selecting this answer confuses the role of the illustration with the role of the claim it illustrates.

### Brief
**Argument breakdown**
- **Conclusion:** It is a mistake to assume that answering what caused the current recession is essential to improving the economy.
- **Evidence:** Corrective lenses effectively treated myopia long before the cause was known to be genetic.
- **Evaluate:** The analogy supports the idea that solutions can precede understanding of root causes. The main conclusion is the columnist's central prescriptive claim about the recession, not the supporting analogy.
- **Goal:** Identify the answer that matches the columnist's main claim: knowing the cause of the recession is not a prerequisite for fixing the economy.

**Answer choices**
**A. Solving a problem never requires finding the root cause of the problem.** — Bad Match (2% of students)
The columnist claims knowing the recession's cause is not essential, not that root causes are never needed for any problem. "Never" makes this far too broad.

**B. Knowing the cause of the current recession would not necessarily enable people to find a solution to it.** — Necessary vs. Sufficient (20% of students)
The columnist says knowing the cause is not necessary (not required). This answer says it would not be sufficient (not enough). Different logical claim — the argument is about what you can skip, not about what might fail.

**C. The question of what caused the current recession is subject to considerable debate.** — Bad Match (1% of students)
This restates background information, not the conclusion. The debate over the recession's cause sets the stage; the conclusion is the columnist's claim that resolving that debate is not essential for economic improvement.

**D. One need not ascertain the cause of the current recession in order to improve the economy.** — Correct (75% of students)
This accurately paraphrases the columnist's central claim: knowing the recession's cause is not a prerequisite for economic improvement. It matches the scope without overstating or understating.

**E. Long before the cause of myopia was known to be genetic, corrective lenses were being used as an effective treatment for the disease.** — Bad Match (1% of students)
This restates the myopia analogy, which is the evidence supporting the conclusion. The conclusion is the claim about the recession; the corrective lenses example is the proof offered for that claim.

### Another Way
**Argument breakdown**
- **Conclusion:** The columnist's big point: stop arguing about what caused the recession and start fixing it, because you do not need to know the cause to find a solution.
- **Evidence:** Exhibit A: eyeglasses. People were correcting myopia with lenses long before anyone figured out that nearsightedness is genetic. The solution came first, the explanation came later. Same logic should apply to the economy.
- **Evaluate:** This is a Main Conclusion question, so the job is to separate the argument's central claim from its evidence and background. The myopia example is evidence, the debate about causes is background, and the actual conclusion is the "it is a mistake" claim. The correct answer should paraphrase that central point without going too far or not far enough.
- **Goal:** Match the columnist's actual conclusion: knowing the cause is not necessary for economic improvement. Dodge the traps that restate the example, overstate the claim, or grab a sub-conclusion.

**Answer choices**
**A. Solving a problem never requires finding the root cause of the problem.** — Bad Match (2% of students)
The columnist made a measured point about the recession. This answer cranks it up to an absolute rule: root causes are NEVER needed. That is like hearing someone say "you do not need an umbrella today" and writing it down as "umbrellas are useless in all weather forever." The columnist is talking about one recession and one economy, not issuing a universal decree about all problem-solving everywhere.

**B. Knowing the cause of the current recession would not necessarily enable people to find a solution to it.** — Necessary vs. Sufficient (20% of students)
Close, but the wrong logical relationship. The columnist says: "You do not NEED to know the cause" (it is not necessary). This answer says: "Even if you knew the cause, it might not help" (it is not sufficient). One is about skipping a step; the other is about whether the step works. Imagine someone says "you do not need a map to find the restaurant." This answer rewrites that as "even with a map you might not find the restaurant." Related territory, but a different claim.

**C. The question of what caused the current recession is subject to considerable debate.** — Bad Match (1% of students)
This is the opening act, not the headliner. The columnist starts by setting the scene — people are arguing about what caused the recession. That is background, the "here is the situation" setup. The actual conclusion is what the columnist argues we should think about that situation: the debate does not need to be resolved before we can fix things. Grabbing the background and calling it the conclusion is like summarizing a movie by describing the opening credits.

**D. One need not ascertain the cause of the current recession in order to improve the economy.** — Correct (75% of students)
Nailed it. The columnist's whole point is: "You do not need to figure out what caused the recession before you can start fixing the economy." This answer says exactly that — no more, no less. It does not overreach into "root causes are never important" territory, it does not confuse the analogy with the conclusion, and it does not grab the background and call it the main point. Goldilocks paraphrase: just right.

**E. Long before the cause of myopia was known to be genetic, corrective lenses were being used as an effective treatment for the disease.** — Bad Match (1% of students)
This is the exhibit in the courtroom, not the verdict. The columnist brought up myopia and corrective lenses to prove a point about the economy — the glasses story is the supporting evidence, the "here is an example" that backs up the real conclusion. Calling this the main conclusion is like reading a lawyer's closing argument and deciding the key point was that exhibit B existed. The myopia story is in service of the recession claim, not the other way around.

# Section 1 (Logical Reasoning)

## S2 · Q20 — Main Conclusion

**Correct answer:** A

> Note: LSAT Lab offers only a single authored written explanation for this question (no Standard / Brief / Another Way selector).

### Stimulus

The public's welfare can be undermined by its own tastes. Journalists tend to focus on stories that will stimulate their readers' interest. Because sensation and drama serve this purpose more successfully than do matter-of-fact descriptions of political or social developments of far-reaching importance, newspaper articles containing the latter are all too often displaced by those that highlight rumors and implausible conspiracies.

### Prompt

Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument above?

### Written (single style)

**Argument breakdown**

*Conclusion:* The public's welfare can be undermined by its own tastes.

*Evidence (for example ...):* Journalists, because they want to focus on stories that stimulate readers, are increasingly doing gossipy stuff rather than hard news.

*Evaluate:* Whenever we do Main Conclusion questions, we prime our brain to read the paragraph in that special way you read Main Conclusion and Role paragraphs —
the conclusion will probably be earlier than the support

Normally, in Logical Reasoning, the Conclusion is more likely to come at the end of the paragraph. But that tendency big time flips on Main Conclusion and Role. So you start listening as early as the very first sentence.

You have to ask yourself actively as you read each claim, "Is this the conclusion? Does it sound like the author's opinion? Does the next sentence start off feeling like it's trying to support this claim?"

On this question, the first sentence doesn't quite sound like an opinion, but it does sound like an abstract claim, rather than a specific fact. Does the next sentence sound like it's supporting this initial claim?

Honestly, no. But if we force ourselves to look closer, there is an overlapping element. They're both talking about "the public's tastes" / "the readers' interest".

The first sentence was positing a causal connection:
public's tastes --> undermines public welfare

This second sentence is talking about the public's taste, when it comes to news stories. Does it say that our taste in news stories leads to "undermining public welfare"?

Yes, aloofly. It goes on to complain that serious news stories have been displaced by TMZ and InfoWars type stories (the author is assuming that this switch in emphasis is something that undermines public welfare, but we don't need to worry about assumptions on Main Conclusion).

Incidentally the "Because" being used in the final sentence should probably be interpreted as a causal usage of Because (as in, "Because I fell down, my knee is bleeding"), not a reasoning usage of Because, as a support indicator.

*Goal:* Our only job is to find the Conclusion. We did. This paragraph made it particularly hard to do so. It's the first sentence. It sure makes life easier if we know the trick for Main Conclusion questions that the conclusion is earlier than the support, the vast majority of the time.

Let's find an answer that mimics the meaning of the first sentence.

**Answer choices**
**A. The best interests of the public sometimes fail to be served because of the sorts of preferences that people have.** — Correct (72% of students)
This is one of those correct answers you'd like to punch.

We were looking for a meaning-match for the first sentence, and this does indeed match the meaning.

```
1st sentence            (A)

The public's welfare            The best interests
                                of the public

can be                          sometimes fail
undermined                      to be served

by its own                      because of the sorts of
tastes                          preferences ppl have
```

This answer's use of the thesaurus is a real [chef's kiss] spice of obnoxious.

Luckily, on Main Conclusion, we always know specifically what claim we're looking for, so if they try to disguise that claim with synonyms we can force ourselves to see through it.

**B. Journalists' tendency to focus on sensational and dramatic stories rather than those of far-reaching importance is to the detriment of the public welfare.** — Not the First Sentence / Assumption (12% of students)
This does not match the first sentence, since it's talking about journalists, who do not appear in the first sentence. So we can eliminate.

For what it's worth, this answer is just presenting an Assumption of the argument, because they know that people will feel its correctness and pick it (after all, it is a correct answer, for a different question type).

**C. Newspaper articles that focus on rumors or speculate about conspiracies too often displace stories about important political or social developments.** — Not the First Sentence / Premise, Last Claim Trap (8% of students)
This does not match the first sentence, since it's talking about newspapers, which do not appear in the first sentence. That's as deep as we need to go.

For what it's worth, this answer is presenting a Premise of the argument, or we could potentially say an Intermediate Conclusion. We know why rumor stories displace serious politics: the public's tastes. So this last claim does feel "supported". But this whole journalism discussion is one big example, which the author is using to support the generalization she made in the first sentence about the public's tastes ending up hurting itself.

Beware picking the last claim as your main conclusion on Main Conclusion. It's usually never there, unless you're doing a very early section easier problem.

**D. The shortcomings of modern print-journalism can be attributed to the preferences of its readers.** — Not the First Sentence / Not Stated (7% of students)
This does not match the first sentence, since it's talking about modern print-journalism, which does not appear in the first sentence. That's as deep as we need to go.

For what it's worth, this answer is also saying something stronger than anything even said in the paragraph. The author has cited one way in which the public's preferences result in something undesirable. But the author hasn't placed sweeping blame like, "All the shortcoming of modern journalism are the fault of readers' preferences"

**E. Journalists should pay more attention to the public's welfare than to its tastes when choosing which stories to focus on.** — Not the First Sentence / Not Stated (1% of students)
This does not match the first sentence, since it's talking about journalists, who aren't mentioned in the first sentence. That's enough to eliminate it.

But this answer is also saying something never expressed in the paragraph. We might speculate that, "If this guy is whining about journalists covering gossip instead of hard news, he would probably say they should pay more attention to what good for people than what people like."

That is far, far from our job on Main Conclusion. We're not speculating other opinions. We're just finding one opinion in the paragraph and picking the answer that matches that opinion.

Furthermore, we can expect our radio telescopes to detect signs of such beings. Alien scientists would have basically the same understanding of mathematics and physics that humans have. Ashley: That is like saying they would inevitably have the same legal or political systems that humans do. Using radio telescopes to search for intelligent life is a waste of time and money.

- Paula: There are lots of Earthlike planets out there, so there's probably intelligent life out there, and we should be able to find such life with radio telescopes. Other intelligent life would have basically the same math / physics that humans have. They'd discover the same fundamental forces of the universe and then develop radio communication.
- Ashley: Saying they'd automatically have the same math / physics / radio technology is like saying (absurdly) that they'd have the same legal or political systems we do. All this stuff is a unique extension of the human form and the Earthly environment. Thus, using radio telescopes to find intelligent life would be pointless.
- Evaluate: I often go claim-by-claim through the first person's statements to see if the 2nd person disagreed with any of the explicit claims.
Here, it seems like Ashley took issue with a couple claims:
- we can expect our radio telescopes to detect signs of such beings
(A would say, "that would be a waste of time and money")
- those smart aliens would have the same math, physics, and radio communication we have.
(A would say, "not necessarily — those are all just outgrowths of our unique physiology")
If we went down to the layer of assumptions, it feels like Paula assumes that "math / physics" are objective properties of the universe that all intelligent life would come to similar conclusions about. Ashley makes those discoveries sound more subjective or contingent on us being us.
- Goal: Look for an answer about whether or not radio telescopes would be likely to detect intelligent life, about whether smart aliens would inevitably find the same (objective) math and physics and technology that we have or whether those things are unique properties of humanity.

[A*] it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have developed radio communication — Correct (60%)
This is the precise point where Paula and Ashley's positions directly conflict. Paula explicitly argues that intelligent aliens would probably develop radio communication — this is the foundation of her case for using radio telescopes. Ashley counters that our scientific and technological development, including radio, is a product of our unique cognitive makeup, implying that aliens would NOT necessarily develop radio. Paula would affirm this proposition; Ashley would deny it. Every other aspect of their arguments — the value of the search, the nature of intelligence, the role of biology — flows from this central factual dispute about whether alien species would arrive at radio technology.

[B] it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have the same legal or political systems that humans do — No Support from Paula (8%)
Ashley mentions legal and political systems as an analogy to illustrate her broader point: just as it would be presumptuous to assume aliens have our legal systems, it is presumptuous to assume they have our science. This is a rhetorical device, not a substantive claim. Paula never addresses alien legal systems at all. For a genuine point of disagreement, both speakers must hold inferable positions on the topic that conflict with each other. Since Paula says nothing about alien legal systems and Ashley raises them only as an analogy, there is no actual dispute on this topic.

[C] our technology is influenced by our cognitive makeup — Both Might Agree (11%)
Ashley's core thesis is that technology is shaped by a species' cognitive and physiological makeup — this is her explicit position. But Paula does not necessarily dispute this general principle. Paula could agree that cognition influences technology while still concluding that, despite cognitive differences, radio communication is a likely convergent development for any intelligent species. Their disagreement is about the specific outcome (whether aliens would develop radio), not about the general principle (whether cognition shapes technology). This answer identifies common ground rather than a point of conflict.

[D] there is likely to be intelligent life on other planets — Out of Scope for Ashley (7%)
Paula assumes intelligent life exists on other planets and argues for a particular search method. Ashley's critique is conditional: even if intelligent aliens exist, we cannot assume they developed radio. She targets the search methodology, not the premise of alien existence. Ashley never expresses skepticism about whether intelligent life exists elsewhere — she simply thinks we are looking for it the wrong way. Without Ashley clearly denying alien existence, this is not a point of disagreement between the two speakers.

[E] scientists should spend more time and money on the search for intelligent extraterrestrial life — Out of Scope for Both (14%)
Neither speaker takes a clear position on whether overall spending on searching for alien life should increase. For a point of disagreement, both speakers must hold inferable and conflicting positions. Their debate is about whether radio is the right approach, not about how much to budget for the search in general.

STIM: Carrillo: Using the number of existing primate species, along with measures of the genetic diversity among these primates and among the extinct primate species, our statistical model strongly supports the conclusion that the first primate developed around 81.5 million years ago. Olson: Given that the oldest primate fossils discovered so far date back only 55 million years, your estimate of how long primate species' development has gone on is sheer speculation.
PROMPT: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Carrillo and Olson disagree over whether
- Carrillo's Claims:   1. Our model strongly supports the conclusion that the first primate developed around 81.5 million years ago.
  2. (implicit): Our model used the number of existing primate species, along with measures of the genetic diversity among these primates and among the primate species.
- Olson's reaction:   1. Your model does not strongly support that conclusion. Your 81.5 million year guess is sheer speculation.
  2. (implicit): I put more faith in our oldest discovered fossils than I do in your statistical model which just used the number of existing primates and the genetic diversity of living and extinct primates.
- Evaluate: This is an unusual Disagree question since the 1st speaker only makes one claim. Lucky for us, that is the claim the 2nd speaker seems to quarrel with, but we have to dial in the language of the disagreement.
- Goal: It looks like it's "strongly support" vs. "sheer speculation", in regards to this statistical model based on quantity and diversity of primate species.
  Though we could also probably say it's a case of "statistical models based on quantity and diversity of primate species" vs. "known fossil evidence", in regards to which type of data is more trustworthy.

[A] primates have been around for more than 55 million years — Unsupported Disagree Position (23%)
We can't support the Disagree position, "Primates have not been around for more than 55 million years". The 2nd speaker isn't saying that 55 million years is definitely the beginning of primates. He's just saying that it's sheer speculation to think it's 81.5 million years ago.

In other words, Olson would say, "I don't know how long primates have been around. It's at least 55 million years, since we have fossils that old, but I do not trust this crazy-different number your statistical model came up with."

[B*] Carrillo's statistical model is a reliable way of dating the first appearance of primate species — Correct (69%)
The notion of whether or not this model is a reliable way speaks to the mismatch we located between "strongly supports" and "sheer speculation".

We can infer that Carrillo would agree because the thinks this model strongly supports a conclusion about the first primates.

And we can infer Olson would disagree since he says, "your estimate is sheer speculation, given a completely different number we get from a more reliable source of information".

[C] the available sample of primate fossils is representative of the variety of primate species that have existed — Both Positions Unsupported (2%)
We can't infer whether either person thinks that the available sample is representative of the variety that have existed, since neither person speaks to that concept.

Carrillo would be the closer one to believing this, but he doesn't need the available sample to be representative for his model to provide strong support. As long as he knows how to weight the un-representativeness of his sample, he can still have an accurate model.

(Pollsters can talk to 2000 people and realize that certain factions of the population are under-represented in their sample, but then they compensate for this by making those data points count for more than just one data point.)

[D] the dating of the primate fossils that Olson cites is accurate — Unsupported Disagree Position (3%)
Olson would probably agree to this, but can we derive that Carrillo would say "those fossils you're referring to have been incorrectly dated at 55 million years old"?

Definitely not. First of all Carrillo never talks about those fossils at all. Secondly, he's only talking about when the first primate developed, not whether the carbon dating on existing fossils was done properly.

[E] fossils of the first primate species that developed have been discovered — Unsupported Agree Position (2%)
We wouldn't be able to derive this from either party's statements. Carrillo, if he trusts his 81 million year estimate and knows that the fossils are 55 million years, might think "those 55 million year old fossils aren't the fossils of the first primate species".

But would Olson say, 'yes they are. The oldest primate fossils discovered so far are fossils of the first primate species'?

We have no idea, but it seems like by saying "so far", Olson is allowing for the possibility that we'll discover even older fossils, so he'd likely be receptive to the possibility that these 55 million year old fossils we have aren't from the very first primate species.

STIM: Bernard: We should not invite Carl to speak at the forum. Carl's views are clearly false, and worse, dangerous.   2. Carl's views are clearly false, and worse, dangerous.
  3. To encourage their consideration will not only legitimize them but also help to promulgate them.
  4. We should avoid legitimizing or promulgating Carl's views, since we wish not to support their adoption.
- Ayla's Responses:   1. Disagrees
  2. no comment
  3. Disagrees
  4. no comment, possibly agrees
- Evaluate: Ayla doesn't explicitly state that Carl should be invited to speak at the forum. However, her statements provide support for the idea that she disagrees with Bernard's first claim and believes that Carl should be allowed to speak. Ayla also doesn't explicitly state that that we should avoid legitimizing or promulgating Carl's views and not support their adoption. However, her statements provide some support for the idea that she agrees with Bernard about this. Ayla talks about combating "false views" and about seeing Carl's views for what they are. Bernard states that Carl's views are false. We can infer that Ayla agrees. They appear to disagree about allowing Carl to speak at the forum. Bernard states that Carl should not be invited, but Ayla appears to suggest that it would be best to allow Carl to speak so that people can publicly challenge his views. "Promulgate" means to promote an idea or make it widely known. If you didn't know this when reading Bernard's statements, but had a sense that it might mean "promote" or "spread," that's totally fine.
- Goal: We'll look for an answer that addresses claim #1 or #3.

[A] one should always avoid legitimizing a view whose adoption one wishes not to support — Too Strong (4%)
The word "always" makes this answer too strong to attribute to either speaker. Bernard argues that Carl's views should not be legitimized, but his argument is specifically about Carl's case. We cannot conclude that Bernard believes one should "always" avoid legitimizing views whose adoption one opposes. Furthermore, even if Bernard did hold this absolute position, Ayla might agree with the general principle — she just thinks that allowing Carl to speak will not actually legitimize his views but rather expose them. Their disagreement is about the consequences of public expression, not about whether one should avoid legitimizing harmful views as a general rule.

[B] people will see the falsity of every dangerous idea for which they are furnished with forceful counterarguments — Too Strong / Half Scope (3%)
The word "every" makes this answer too strong. Ayla suggests that public scrutiny at the forum will produce convincing arguments against Carl's views, allowing people to see them for what they are. But we cannot conclude that Ayla believes this works for "every" dangerous idea. She may only believe this about Carl's particular views or about the particular forum being discussed. Additionally, Ayla calls Carl's views "false" but never calls them "dangerous" — that is Bernard's characterization. We do not know whether Ayla considers Carl's views dangerous, so any answer involving "dangerous" ideas is at best a half-scope match for Ayla's position.

[C*] the best way to fight erroneous ideas involves allowing the public expression of these ideas — Correct (90%)
This answer captures the core disagreement. Bernard believes that allowing Carl to speak at the forum would legitimize and help spread his views — meaning public expression of erroneous ideas is counterproductive. Ayla believes the opposite: "the best way to combat false views is to challenge them in public," which requires allowing their public expression. Bernard opposes public expression of false views as a means of fighting them; Ayla endorses it. This is a clean disagreement where both speakers hold clear, opposing positions on whether allowing public expression of erroneous ideas is an effective strategy for combating them.

[D] people who hold false views tend to pose a danger to society — Too Strong / Half Scope (1%)
Bernard says Carl's views are "false, and worse, dangerous," but this does not mean he believes there is a general tendency for people with false views to pose a danger to society. He is making a specific claim about Carl, not a generalization about all people with false views. Even if we could attribute this general belief to Bernard, we do not know Ayla's position on it. Ayla acknowledges that Carl's views are false but never addresses whether false views generally make their holders dangerous to society. Without clear positions from both speakers, this cannot be the point at issue.

[E] one should not encourage the adoption of dangerous views — Half Scope (1%)
Both Bernard and Ayla appear to agree with this statement, or at least neither clearly disagrees. Bernard argues against legitimizing and promulgating Carl's views "since we wish not to support their adoption," which aligns with not encouraging adoption of dangerous views. Ayla discusses combating "false views" and seeing them "for what they are," which also suggests she opposes their adoption. Since both speakers appear to be on the same side of this proposition, it is not a point of disagreement. Additionally, Ayla never uses the word "dangerous" — she discusses "false views" — so attributing a position about "dangerous" views to her is unsupported.

## S3 · Q5 — Flaw

**Correct answer:** E

> Note: LSAT Lab offers only a single authored written explanation for this question (no Standard / Brief / Another Way selector). This question's Written explanation shows no left-panel argument breakdown, only per-choice analysis.

### Stimulus
Jenkins maintains that the movie Firepower was not intended to provoke antisocial behavior, arguing that, on the contrary, it is in the interest of Firepower's director to prevent such behavior. Yet Jenkins's conclusion must be rejected, because the movie has clearly produced antisocial behavior among many of those who have seen it.

### Prompt
The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that it

### Written (single style)
**Answer choices**
**A. rejects an argument on the grounds that it was offered by a person who was biased** — Not Ad Hominem / Bad Evidence Match (1% of students)
This refers to the famous Ad Hominem flaw, in which someone dismisses a point of view because the source of the view has a biased interest (or because the source has some conflicting past behavior).

This author does reject an argument, in her conclusion.

But the grounds on which she does so (i.e. the evidence) isn't a claim about the bias of Jenkins.

Rather, the evidence is a claim that "many who've seen this movie were caused to act antisocially".

**B. concludes from a mere correlation between certain phenomena that those phenomena are causally related** — Not Correlation vs. Causation / Bad Evidence Match (15% of students)
This refers to the famous Causal Overconfidence flaw, in which an author overconfidently concludes one possible causal explanation for something, without ruling out other possible explanations.

Any time a Flaw answer is structured
concludes from X that Y
then we can ask ourselves if X matches the evidence and Y matches the conclusion.

Was the evidence "a mere correlation between phenomena"?

No, the evidence was "the movie has clearly produced antisocial behavior among many who have seen it". That verb 'produced' makes this a causal statement, not a correlation.

We could also say that the conclusion is not a causal claim; it's just saying that "the movie was intended to provoke antisocial behavior".

That's talking about whether or not a certain motive existed; it's not claiming that Thing 1 caused Thing 2.

**C. infers that something is true of a whole solely on the grounds that it is true of a part of the whole** — Not Part vs. Whole / Bad Evidence Match (3% of students)
This refers to the famous Part vs. Whole flaw, in which an author assumes that a trait that applies to a collective group also applies to each member within the group (or vice versa).
