=========== PT155-S1-Q23 [single] Weaken d5 777w | Explain Curious Fact; EXCEPT; Science | Causation
STIM: On Earth, biological activity leads to a change in the ratio of isotope S-34 to isotope S-32. However, a newly discovered meteorite of Martian origin exhibits ratios of these elements found only in terrestrial minerals dating from before the beginning of life on Earth. Therefore, it is unlikely that life occurred on Mars.
PROMPT: Each of the following, if true, would weaken the argument except:
- Conclusion (Therefore): It is unlikely that life occurred on Mars.
- Evidence: On Earth, life leads to a change in the ratio of isotope S-34 to S-32.
  A new meteorite that came from Mars shows ratios of these elements found only in terrestrial minerals dating from before the beginning of life on Earth (i.e. the meteorite has the pre-life ratio of 34 to 32)
- Evaluate: The author is thinking that if Mars had had life, then that life would have converted the S-34 to S-32 ratio. And then if a meteorite came from Mars to Earth, then it would be showing that post-life ratio.
  Since the meteorite that came from Mars showed the pre-life ratio, the author is concluding that there was never life on Mars.
  Given that ... this meteorite has the pre-life ratio we see on Earth
  How could we still argue that ... life did occur on Mars?
  Maybe on Earth biological life changes the ratio, but on Mars it doesn't, so even if there was life it would have still been the same ratio.
  Maybe there was life on some areas of Mars and it changed the isotope ratio in those areas, but this meteorite came from a life-free part of Mars, so it shows the pre-life ratio.
- Goal: Since this is an EXCEPT, there are going to be four answers that weaken. We aren't going to anticipate all four. We just want to set up our brains to interpret these answers. They fit into either of these sentences:
  "Life did occur on Mars. The reason that meteorite only shows the pre-life ratio is because ...."
  "Yes, the meteorite from Mars had the pre-life isotope ratio. But, it's still likely that life occurred on Mars, because ..."

[A] Life forms that have a different effect on the ratio of S-34 to S-32 from that of life forms on Earth could have evolved elsewhere. — Weakens (7%)
"Life did occur on Mars. The reason that this Martian meteorite only shows the pre-life ratio is because ...."

.... life forms that have evolved on other planets, unlike those on Earth, don't change the ratio of S-34 to S-32.

[B] The effects of life on the ratio of S-34 to S-32 depend on a number of climatic and environmental factors with regard to which Earth and Mars differ. — Weakens (10%)
"Life did occur on Mars. The reason that this Martian meteorite only shows the pre-life ratio is because ... "

.... life forms don't necessarily change the ratio from S-34 to S-32; it's complicated; it's based on some other climate and environmental factors that are different on Earth vs. Mars.

This is essentially the same as (A). We're able to argue that on Mars, life doesn't change the ratio of S-34 to S-32 because of different climate and environmental factors, so that's why even though there was life on Mars, the Martian meteorite won't show the ratio that happens on Earth when life comes on the scene.

[C*] The ratio of S-34 to S-32 in the meteorite is the same as that on Mars as a whole at the time that the material in the meteorite left Mars. — Correct: strengthens (53%)
One of our possible objections was that "There was life on some spots of Mars, and in those spots the ratio changed as it did on Earth. But ... this meteorite happened to come from a different spot of Mars, where life had not affected the ratio."

This answer strengthens by ruling out that objection.

It's saying that the ratio in the meteorite was fully representative of the ratio present on Mars when that meteorite left.

[D] Relatively few terrestrial mineral samples contain S-34 and S-32 in the ratio that indicates the presence of biological activity. — Weakens (16%)
"Life did occur on Mars. The reason that this Martian meteorite shows a pre-life ratio is that ...

.... life doesn't usually change the isotope ratio when it comes to terrestrial minerals.

STIM: More pedestrian injuries occur at crosswalks marked by both striping on the roadway and flashing lights than occur at crosswalks not so marked. Obviously these so-called safety features are a waste of taxpayer money.
PROMPT: 7. The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism because the argument
- Conclusion: - These so-called safety features are a waste of taxpayer money.
- Evidence: - More pedestrian injuries occur at crosswalks with striping and flashing lights than at those without.
- Evaluate: - The argument ignores that the marked crosswalks may be more dangerous to begin with.
- Goal: - Find the flaw that mistakes a response to danger for a cause of danger.

[A*] fails to consider that crosswalks marked by both striping and flashing lights are marked in this way precisely because they are the most dangerous ones — Correct (86%)
This is the flaw.

[B] takes for granted that safety features that fail to reduce the number of injuries are a waste of taxpayer money — Bad Evidence Match / Not a Good Objection (6%)
There is no before/after evidence.

[C] presumes that there are less expensive features that will reduce the number of pedestrian injuries just as effectively as striping and flashing lights — Out of Scope: less expensive (4%)
Cost alternatives are irrelevant.

[D] takes for granted that crosswalks with both striping and flashing lights have no other safety features — Too Strong: no other features (3%)
That is unnecessary.

[E] fails to consider that, in accidents involving pedestrians and cars, the injuries to pedestrians are nearly always more serious than the injuries to occupants of cars — Not an Objection (1%)
This is irrelevant to the argument.

STIM: Government official: Although the determination of local residents to rebuild hiking trails recently devastated by a landslide indicates that they are strongly committed to their community, the government should not assist them in rebuilding. The reason is clear: there is a strong likelihood of future landslides in that location that could cause serious injury or worse.
PROMPT: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in the government official's argument?
- Conclusion (should not = opinion): The government should not assist in rebuilding trails that have been washed out by landslides.
- Evidence: There is a strong likelihood that future landslides could cause serious injury if the trails are rebuilt, thereby posing a risk to users.
- Evaluate: We can predict an "If Evidence, then Conclusion" answer on Principle-Strengthen.
"If an action would lead to a strong likelihood of injury or worse, then the government shouldn't assist that action".
- Goal: Look for an answer that aligns with both the conclusion's normative stance about what the government "should not assist" and the evidence concerning risk.

[A] Residents should not be allowed to rebuild trails unless the government assists them in rebuilding. — Bad Conclusion Match (0%)
This choice discusses what residents should not be allowed to do, rather than focusing on government actions. It doesn't align with the conclusion about government responsibilities.

[B] The determination of residents to rebuild hiking trails devastated by landslides should be what determines government support for the project. — Opposite (if anything) (0%)
This sounds more like, "If residents are determined to rebuild, then government SHOULD support it".

[C] Government agencies should not assist people with projects unless those people are strongly committed to their community. — Bad Trigger Match (0%)
This rule says, "if people are not strongly committed to their community, govt should not assist with projects".

The outcome matches our conclusion, but the trigger doesn't apply to our evidence. The situation actually indicates people with a strong commitment to their community, making this trigger irrelevant to the current evidence.

[D*] The government should not assist in projects that are very likely to result in circumstances that could lead to serious injury. — Correct (97%)
This provides a principle stating that if a project is very likely to result in serious injury, the government should not assist. It accurately covers the given evidence of strong likelihood of injury and aligns with the conclusion by stating the government's role is not to assist in this context.

[E] Residents should be discouraged from rebuilding in any area that has had an extensive history of landslides. — Bad Conclusion Match (2%)
Similar to (A), this addresses residents rather than specifying government actions, thus irrelevant to the issue of government involvement in rebuilding high-risk trails.

=========== PT151-S2-Q18 [single] Strengthen d5 117w | Explain Curious Fact | Comparative Reasoning
STIM: In grasslands near the Namib Desert there are "fairy circles"—large, circular patches that are entirely devoid of vegetation. Since sand termite colonies were found in every fairy circle they investigated, scientists hypothesize that it is the burrowing activities of these termites that cause the circles to form.
PROMPT: Which one of the following, if true, most supports the scientists' hypothesis?
- Conclusion: Sand termite burrowing causes fairy circles to form.
- Evidence: Sand termite colonies were found in every investigated fairy circle.
- Evaluate: The argument leans on a correlation. To strengthen, link the actual damage pattern to termite burrowing.
- Goal: Pick the answer that shows fairy-circle damage is consistent with termite burrowing activity.

[A*] Dying grass plants within newly forming fairy circles are damaged only at the roots. — Correct (52%)
Damage only at the roots fits termite burrowing — an underground cause matching the proposed mechanism.

[B] The grasses that grow around fairy circles are able to survive even the harshest and most prolonged droughts in the region. — Opposite (10%)
Drought-resistant surrounding grasses cut against, not for, the termite hypothesis.

[C] The soil in fairy circles typically has higher water content than the soil in areas immediately outside the circles. — No Impact (3%)
Higher water content does not specifically implicate termite burrowing as the cause.

[D] Fairy circles tend to form in areas that already have numerous other fairy circles. — No Impact (6%)
Clustering is consistent with many causes; it does not specifically support termites.

[E] Species of animals that feed on sand termites are often found living near fairy circles. — No Impact (29%)
Predators near circles only re-confirms termite presence; it does not show termite burrowing causes the circles.

=========== PT155-S2-Q10 [single] Paradox d3 304w | Plans / Recommendations | Causation; Comparative Reasoning
STIM: Toning shoes—walking shoes with a specially rounded sole—are popular with fitness enthusiasts. Research shows that the major leg muscles of people walking in toning shoes receive no more exercise than those of people walking in ordinary walking shoes. Nevertheless, many people experience a strengthening of their major leg muscles after switching to toning shoes.
PROMPT: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?
- Background: Research shows that the major leg muscles of people walking in toning shoes receive no more exercise than those of people walking in normal walking shoes.
- Surprising Claim: Many people experience a strengthening of their major leg muscles after switching to toning shoes.
- Evaluate: Given that studies show the shoes themselves don't actually exercise the major leg muscles more, what else could be different about people who switched to toning shoes? Maybe they get more excited to exercise or motivated, since they see themselves wearing athletic gear?
- Goal: Find something else that's happening with the people who switched that would explain why they experience a strengthening of major leg muscles.

[A] Toning shoes strengthen small underused muscles in the feet and ankles. — Out of Scope: small muscles (16%)
We're looking for a way to explain why major muscles are strengthening.

[B] Muscles in the leg adapt to the rounded shape of toning shoes almost immediately. — No Impact (5%)
Adapting immediately sounds more like the research's takeaway — these end up being the same as regular shoes.

Nothing in this answer gives us a way to explain why the major leg muscles are getting strengthened.

[C*] Many people find toning shoes especially comfortable and walk more as a result. — Correct (77%)
If they walk more as a result, that could explain why they experience a strengthening of their major leg muscles.

It would be like if you got new headphones, and listening to music was so enjoyable that you walked more, and so we said that "the new headphones helped you to strengthen your major leg muscles".

The headphones don't directly exercise your major leg muscles more, but they lead you to exercise your major leg muscles more.

[D] There is little evidence that toning shoes cause injuries to their wearers. — No Impact (0%)
The fact that these shoes don't cause injuries doesn't give us a good way to explain why there is more major leg muscle strengthening being experienced by those who switch to toning shoes.

[E] Shoes that strengthen the major leg muscles are more marketable than ordinary shoes. — Out of Scope: marketable (1%)
We don't care about how well these shoes do / don't sell. We're just wondering why those who wear them, however big or small that number is, are experiencing a strengthening of major leg muscles.

=========== PT153-S2-Q11 [single] Most Supported d2 309w | Causal Difference-Maker | Comparative Reasoning
STIM: Unlike other mechanical devices, the clock did not evolve from the simple to the complex. The earliest clocks were also the most complicated. This is because early clocks were used primarily to predict astronomical phenomena, though the mechanisms they used for this purpose incidentally enabled one to keep track of time. Gradually the timekeeping functions became more important and the astronomical ones diminished.
PROMPT: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
- Statements: Clocks are sort of unique, in that they started out more complex and got simple over time. This is because (causal difference-maker language), clocks were originally made to predict astronomical stuff, and time-keeping was just an afterthought. Over time, clocks were mainly about time-keeping and less about astronomical stuff.
- Evaluate: When we see Contrasts and Causal Difference-Maker language, we're usually trying to spell out some sense of, "This difference causes that difference". We have two parallel timelines here:
```
Earlier              Later
clocks primarily     clocks primarily
for astronomy        for time-keeping
clocks more          clocks simpler
complex
```
- Goal: We'll probably see an an answer that connects "Making clocks primarily for astronomy makes them more complex" or "Keeping time is simpler than predicting astronomical phenomena"

[A] Present-day clocks are of no use in the prediction of astronomical phenomena. — Too Strong: no use (4%)
The last sentence only says that "astronomical functions have diminished in importance", not totally disappeared.

[B] The mechanisms used to predict astronomical phenomena in at least some clocks were more complicated than most more recent mechanisms used for this function. — Unknown Comparison (5%)
We can't compare "astronomical mechanisms" before to astronomical mechanisms now. We can compare clocks then to clocks now, but to the extent that clocks have preserved any of the astronomical mechanisms, those individual mechanisms might be the same.

The clocks today might be simpler by just containing fewer mechanisms used to predict astronomical phenomena.

[C] Clocks used only for keeping time do not differ appreciably in their mechanical complexity. — Unknown Comparison (4%)
We can compare clocks from before to clocks now, but we can't say something as strong as "clocks used only to keep time are pretty much all equally complex".

[D*] The mechanisms that the earliest clocks used to predict astronomical phenomena were more complicated than the mechanisms used for timekeeping functions in some more recent clocks. — Correct (83%)
This seems to reinforce the story we told, that as clocks went from primarily predicting astronomical phenomena to primarily keeping time, they went from more complex to more simple.

The internal logic of that progression is that it's simpler to keep time than to predict astronomical functions.

[E] Interest in predicting astronomical phenomena has declined steadily since the invention of the first mechanical clocks. — Out of Scope: interest in predicting (5%)
We're only learning about the evolving functions of clocks. We might be able to say that interest in having a clock predict astronomical phenomena has declined, but we can't say that overall societal/scientific interest in predicting astronomical phenomena has steadily declined.

=========== PT155-S4-Q14 [single] Necessary Assumption d3 333w | First Sentence Conclusion; Missing Link / Idea; New Concept in Conclusion; Untriggered Conditional | Conditional Reasoning
STIM: Deborra: The art of still photography cannot enable us to understand the world. After all, understanding starts from refusing to accept the world as it looks and inquiring into the world's reality, and the reality of the world is not in its images but in its functions. PROMPT: Which one of the following is an assumption on which Deborra's argument depends?
- Conclusion: The art of still photography can't enable us to understand the world.
- Evidence: ```
Accept the world as it
looks or Don't inquire    →  can't understand
into the world's reality     world
```
  Reality ≠ images. Reality = functions.
```
Doesn't narrate → can't help us understand
```
- Evaluation: Lots of potholes here, so it's hard to predict which one the answer might fill.
  The art of still photography is a New Term in the Conclusion and thus will almost certainly be in the correct answer.
  We are assuming that still photography does not involve refusing to accept the world as it looks.
  We're assuming that still photography does not involve inquiring into the world's reality.
  We're assuming that still photography only lets us see images, not functions.
  We're assuming that still photography doesn't narrate.
- Goal: Look for one of the four missing links.

[A] Artists who take still photographs do not attempt to understand the world. — Too Strong: don't attempt (2%)
It doesn't hurt the author's argument if still photographers attempt to understand the world. The author is ultimately saying their attempt will be futile, but it doesn't hurt the author to say that they're attempting.

[B] The functioning of the world cannot be captured on film. — Too Broad: captured on film (16%)
The author is assuming that "still photography" does not convey the functioning of the world.

But moving photography (i.e. films), might be something the author believes can convey the functioning of the world.

[C*] The art of still photography is not narrative. — Correct (79%)
The author's first claim, her conclusion, says:
```
Still Photography → can't help understand
```

Her last claim, one of her premises says:
```
doesn't narrate → can't help understand
```

So she's assuming:
```
Still Photography → doesn't narrate → can't help understand
```

If we negated this, it would sound like a big objection to follow-up on the author's last claim.

AUTHOR: only that which narrates can enable us to understand.

NEGATED (C): cool, well still photography does narrate!

[D] A complete understanding of the world is not attainable through art. — Too Strong: not attainable through art (2%)
This argument is just about what still photography can't do, not about what the whole of art can / can't do.

[E] Images cannot be properly explained. — Out of Scope: properly explained (2%)
There's no language like "properly explained" when it comes to images.

Properly explaining an image ≠ understanding the world.

STIM: Manager: The only employees who should receive bonuses this year are those who were exceptionally productive over the past year. Liang is an excellent account executive, but she works in a corporate division that has failed to meet its productivity goals for the year. Thus Liang should not receive a bonus this year.
PROMPT: The reasoning in the manager's argument is flawed in that the argument
- Evidence: The only employees who should receive bonuses this year are those who were exceptionally productive over the past year.
  Liang works in a division that has failed to meet its productivity goals for the year.
- Conclusion: Liang should not receive a bonus this year.
- Evaluate: The evidence would provide more support for this conclusion if the second premise stated that Liang failed to meet her productivity goals for the year. But we're only told that the division that Liang works in failed to meet its goals. The argument assumes that what is true of the division is also true for Liang. That's not necessarily the case.

Or is she an unrepresentative sample of someone who started at the bottom and made it all the way to the top?" STIM: Industrial engineer: Some people have suggested that the problem of global warming should be addressed by pumping some of the carbon dioxide produced by the burning of fossil fuels into the deep ocean. - Conclusion: The worry that dumping fossil fuel’s CO2 into the ocean would trade one pollution for another equally bad one is unfounded.
- Evidence: Tons of the CO2 that comes from fossil fuels already ends up in the ocean, and it’s not causing any environmental problems as bad as global warming.
- Evaluation: This follows a classic template for Main Conclusion questions in which you hear a Counterpoint, hear the author’s disagreeing Conclusion, and then hear the author’s support for that disagreement.
- Goal: We just need a paraphrase of “Environmentalists don’t have good reason to worry that dumping CO2 in the ocean would trade one pollution for an equally bad one.”

[B] Environmentalists worry that the strategy of pumping carbon dioxide into the deep ocean to reduce global warming would simply exchange one form of pollution for :: This is the claim that our Main Conclusion is fighting.
[C*] Worrying that pumping carbon dioxide into the deep ocean to reduce global warming would simply exchange one form of pollution for another, equally destructive,  :: Pretty friendly answer in that it actually uses the wording “worry is unfounded” and just inserts the borrowed wording of the previous sentence.
[D] Much of the carbon dioxide now released into the atmosphere ends up in the ocean where it does not cause environmental disturbances as destructive as global war :: This is the author’s premise.
[E] To reduce global warming, the strategy of pumping into the deep ocean at least some of the carbon dioxide now released into the atmosphere should be considered. :: This is the trap of thinking, “What might the author say next?” We’re just supposed to be identifying the explicit conclusion on the page. Maybe if you think “worrying about X is unfounded”, then your next thought would be, “so we should do X”, but maybe not. Either way, we’re not being tested on what else the author might believe. Make sure your correct answer traces back to a specific claim that was made in the argument.

=== PT126-S4-Q20 [single] Weaken (Weaken) d3 258w | Argue the Anti-Conclusion | Conditional Reasoning
STIM: People who have specialized knowledge about a scientific or technical issue are systematically excluded from juries for trials where that issue is relevant. Thus, trial by jury is not a fair means of settling disputes involving such issues.

- Conclusion (Thus): A jury trial is not a fair means of settling disputes involving scientific or technical issues.
- Evidence: People with specialized knowledge about the issues are excluded from juries, if that issue is relevant.
- Evaluate: We can apply our generic Weaken template to this argument: GIVEN THAT people with specialized knowledge are excluded from juries if the case involves that specialty, HOW CAN WE ARGUE THAT jury trials are still fair, when they deal with specialized subjects/ To weaken the argument, we can counter the negative perception of excluding specialists or argue that fairness is achieved through other means.
- Goal: Identify an answer choice that supports the idea of fairness in jury trials by highlighting the benefits of excluding specialists or reinforcing the ability of jurors to reach fair decisions.
[A] The more complicated the issue being litigated, the less likely it is that a juror without specialized knowledge of the field involved will be able to comprehen :: This suggests regular jurors struggle with complex issues, implying that excluding specialists worsens trial fairness by leaving juries ill-equipped, thereby supporting the need for specialists.
[B*] The more a juror knows about a particular scientific or technical issue involved in a trial, the more likely it is that the juror will be prejudiced in favor of :: This argues that jurors with specialized knowledge are more likely to be prejudiced, suggesting that excluding them may actually enhance fairness by removing potential bias, countering the argument against jury trials.
[C] Appointing an impartial arbitrator is not a fair means of settling disputes involving scientific or technical issues, because arbitrators tend to favor settleme :: This introduces arbitrators, which are outside the scope of the discussion focused on jury trials, making it an irrelevant consideration here.

[E] Expert witnesses in specialized fields often command fees that are so high that many people involved in litigation cannot afford their services. :: This highlights the costs of expert witnesses, which doesn’t relate to the inclusion of knowledgeable individuals on juries, thus straying from the core claim about trial fairness.

I did not trust the bank's `questionType`: in the PT139-159 overlap it disagrees with the file label on 224 of 1,234 questions, and many of those are a default \"Most Strongly Supported\" on questions that are plainly Flaw, Paradox or Role.\n\n**Data problems found (not fixed, reported only).**\n- The local `Explanations/PT140-explanations.md` is a thin, different version: about 100 words per question against about 630 in the DB. All 69 PT140 overlaps differ; every other PT139-159 question matches the DB within 20 words. Anyone reading PT140 from the markdown sees the wrong text.\n- Bank alignment: 110 explained DB questions have no matching bank entry at the same PT/section/question, and 27 match a bank entry filed under another number (for example, the local PT148-S4-Q24 to Q26 stimuli sit in the bank under PT149-S4-Q24 to Q26). Features and difficulty for those are missing or borrowed; the inventory column `bank_match` says which.\n- Transcription damage recurs in diagrams: arrow diagrams flattened onto one line (PT139-S4-Q8, PT139-S4-Q21), and in PT144-S2-Q22 the negation marks were lost so two diagrams now read backwards.\n- Leftover source references: \"try this one\" pointing at a missing link (PT139-S1-Q5), \"Welcome to Test 89\" (PT155-S4-Q15).\n- The bank carries a \"Games-y LR\" feature tag (for example PT119-S4-Q24). Worth knowing given the no-Logic-Games rule for student copy.\n\n## 2. Quality by test range\n\n| PTs | Explained | Avg words | Complete | Em-dashes per 1k words | Notes |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 101-122 | 1,158 | 553 | 85% | 0.5 | Full LSAT Lab voice. Many golden picks come from here. |\n| 123-138 | 1,025 | 362 | 51% | 0.7 | Noticeably thinner. Most \"incomplete\" rows have a breakdown but no Goal step (346), and choice notes are often one or two lines. Some notes read like generic summaries (PT126-S4-Q20: \"This introduces arbitrators, which are outside the scope\"). |\n| 139-156 | 1,097 | 588 | 91% | 0.6 | Same voice as 101-122. Consistently strong. |\n| 157-159 | 139 | 672 | 89% | 7.1 | PT157/158 are explicit Standard. Breakdowns are in the house voice; choice notes are a different register (below). |\n\n**The PT157/158 explicit-Standard register.** Choice notes run about 100+ words each, open with formulas (\"This answer captures...\", \"This answer identifies the argument's central flaw\"), use em-dashes at roughly ten times the rate of everything else, and repeat the same point several ways. More importantly, they contain accuracy slips I did not find in the single-style text at the same rate:\n- PT158-S3-Q2: the D note describes a different answer (\"can effectively combine knowledge\") from the actual choice (\"can effectively solve many problems\"); A is tagged \"No Impact\" while its note argues it undermines the argument.\n- PT158-S2-Q16: the correct-answer note imports outside history (Plato's family wealth, Philip of Macedon) to justify the answer.\n- PT158-S2-Q18: the A note argues against a claim the choice does not make.\n\nThat is why no explicit-Standard item made the golden set, and why the house voice rules (no em-dashes) matter for the writing guide.\n\n**Two voices inside the single style.** Most text is one conversational author (voice A: \"Hey, author\", \"Let's look for\", FABS, Curious Fact, Given that / How can it be that). A second, more formal author appears in about 15% of questions (voice B: \"Beware of answers that...\", \"If you chose this answer...\", \"This answer choice...\"). Voice B is accurate and structured but lighter on prediction and analogy. Examples: PT146-S2-Q8, PT151-S2-Q1, PT152-S4-Q5, PT154-S1-Q10, PT155-S4-Q1. Both voices can produce a strong explanation; voice A produces most of the best ones.\n\n## 3. What separates strong from loose (the empirical comparison)\n\nI picked ten explanations that were clearly strong and ten that were complete but loose, read all twenty side by side, then measured a few things.\n\n- **Strong (10):** PT139-S4-Q18 Flaw, PT142-S4-Q22 Flaw, PT145-S2-Q19 Paradox, PT154-S1-Q18 NA, PT153-S2-Q13 Weaken, PT146-S2-Q13 Strengthen, PT147-S1-Q17 Evaluate, PT152-S2-Q21 Principle-Conform, PT150-S3-Q15 Agree/Disagree, PT144-S3-Q17 Role.\n- **Loose but complete (10), with the failure each shows:** PT127-S2-Q3 Weaken (two wrong answers get one line each: \"This supports the argument's explanation\"); PT126-S4-Q20 Weaken (generic summary notes, a Goal that restates the task); PT124-S3-Q10 Role (short, and \"Haha. This answer is unthinkably weird\"); PT151-S2-Q18 Strengthen (117 words total; the 29% trap gets one sentence); PT146-S2-Q8 Flaw (every wrong answer is \"The argument never discusses X\", correct note is one line); PT142-S4-Q5 Principle (mechanical, no reason why the trap tempts); PT155-S2-Q10 Paradox (fine idea, thin notes); PT158-S3-Q2 Strengthen (long, but misquotes a choice); PT158-S2-Q16 Paradox (long, but brings in outside facts); PT148-S1-Q20 Method (sound analysis, but calls the correct answer \"so, so dumb\").\n\nMeasured averages (strong vs loose):\n\n| Measure | Strong | Loose |\n|---|---|---|\n| Total words | 773 | 394 |\n| Words in the Evaluate step | 169 | 77 |\n| Words in the Goal step | 66 | 43 |\n| Goal names 3+ content words from the stimulus | 0.9 | 0.5 |\n| Avg words per wrong-answer note | 87 | 45 |\n| Wrong-answer notes under 20 words (verdict only) | 0.0 per question | 1.1 per question |\n| Wrong-answer notes that run an explicit test (negate it, does it weaken, does it trigger the rule, why should we believe it) | 1.4 of 4 | 0.2 of 4 |\n| Words in the correct-answer note | 143 | 60 |\n| Examples, analogies or worked numbers | 2.0 | 0.5 |\n| Stated generalizations (\"whenever\", \"on X questions\", \"usually\") | 1.6 | 0.3 |\n\nWhat actually separates them, in order of how reliably it predicted my judgment:\n\n1. **The Evaluate step argues with the argument.** Strong ones do real work before the choices: they build the objection (\"Given that X, how could we argue not-Y?\"), do the arithmetic (25% of $400 vs 13% of $1,000), or set the two populations side by side. Loose ones restate the stimulus and move on.\n2. **The Goal names the answer, not the task.** Strong: \"look for an answer saying the fish in the leafless trees are exposed to predators that hunt by sight.\" Loose: \"Find the flaw that mistakes a response to danger for a cause\", \"Identify an answer choice that supports fairness.\" Strong Goals often give two acceptable shapes (a linking answer or a defender).\n3. **Every wrong answer gets a reason tied to this question, and usually a test.** The loose group's signature is the verdict-only note: \"This is irrelevant.\", \"That is unnecessary.\", \"The argument never discusses profits.\" Strong notes say what the answer claims, what was needed, and where they diverge, often by running the family's test on it (negate it; would it weaken; is the trigger established; does the conclusion match the rule's right side).\n4. **The popular trap gets the most attention.** Strong explanations spend their longest wrong-answer note on the choice that drew 15-30% of students and say why it tempts. Loose ones treat it like every other wrong answer.\n5. **The correct-answer note explains the fit, and often generalizes it.** Strong: \"Another correct answer performing the same function could have said...\" (PT146-S2-Q13); the karaoke/Jenga reason why A → C still works when you predicted A and B → C (PT139-S4-Q21). Loose: \"This is the flaw.\"\n6. **Fidelity.** Two loose items are long. Length did not save them: a misquoted answer choice, imported outside facts, or the author disowning the question destroys model value regardless of word count.\n\nWhat did not separate them: word count by itself (PT152-S4-Q19 is 479 words and strong; PT158-S2-Q16 is 716 and loose), the choice-tag vocabulary, and the presence of jokes (several strong ones joke; it only hurts when the joke is at the question's or the answer's expense).\n\n## 4. Rubric used for the shortlist\n\nGate (hard requirement): full Argument breakdown and all five choice notes. Every shortlisted candidate passed.\n\nScored 0 / 1 / 2:\n\n| Criterion | 2 | 1 | 0 |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **P** Prediction | Goal names the content or shape of the right answer before the choices (may give two acceptable shapes) | Goal names the task or admits it cannot predict | No prediction |\n| **X** Precision | Names the exact gap, flaw or relationship in this argument's words | Uses the right label but stays generic | Label only, or wrong |\n| **E** Eliminations | Every wrong answer gets a question-grounded reason; the popular trap gets the most attention | Most do; one or two verdict-only notes | Verdict-only notes |\n| **T** Transfer | States the move in a form that works on the next question of this type (the test, the rule, the recurring trap) | Transfer is implicit | None |\n| **C** Clarity | Plain, no padding, no pasted repetition | Some padding or pasted notes | Hard to follow |\n| **L** Learner value | Teaches what a student needs to understand and repeat the move: why the trap tempts, what to do when stuck, a worked example or analogy, a second correct answer that would also work | Justifies the key well but does not teach the move | Only justifies the key |\n\nPlus a **fidelity flag** (not scored; disqualifying if serious): `slip` factual or typo error, `tone` the author mocks the question or answer, `register` explicit-Standard PT157/158 prose, `transcription` damaged text.\n\nLearner value is the criterion that most often separated a 10 from a 12. Many explanations justify the key correctly (1) but only the best ones also show the student the move they will reuse (2).\n\n## 5. Step structure per family (DB, most common sequences)\n\nLabels normalized (parenthetical indicator words dropped: \"Conclusion (therefore)\" counts as Conclusion).\n\n- **Flaw (524):** Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (67%); Evidence > Conclusion > Evaluate (9%); with an Intermediate Conclusion step (5%). Evaluate usually names the famous flaw or builds the objection; Goal often gives both the formal and the \"fails to consider\" phrasing.\n- **Must Be True / Most Supported (462):** Statements > Evaluate > Goal (45%); Statements only (16%). Statements is often a diagram. Evaluate scans for conditional, causal, math and pivot wording and names the inference to make.\n- **Necessary Assumption (352):** Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (66%). Goal typically offers a linking answer and a defender answer, and says \"negate it\".\n- **Weaken (335) / Strengthen (277):** Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (59% / 55%). Evaluate uses \"Given that ... how could we argue that ...\" or Curious Fact / Alternate Explanation / Plausibility.\n- **Paradox (213):** \"Apparent Paradox > Evaluate\" (22%, older tests) or \"Given that ... > How can it be that / Why is it that ... > Evaluate > Goal\" (about 30% combined, often with Evaluate / Goal merged).\n- **Sufficient Assumption (193):** Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (53%); Evidence > Conclusion > Evaluate (21%). Goal usually diagrams the missing link as the logic path.\n- **Principle-Strengthen (181):** Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (48%). Goal is \"If evidence, then conclusion\" in general terms.\n- **Principle-Conform (99):** mixed. Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (24%) when the principle is in the answers; Principle > Evaluate > Goal (9%) or Principle > Goal (7%) when it is in the stimulus.\n- **Main Conclusion (144) / Role (126):** Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (42% / 53%), with an Intermediate Conclusion step in about 8%. Evaluate almost always opens with the reminder that the conclusion usually comes early (first sentence or after a pivot).\n- **Parallel (100) / Parallel Flaw (123):** Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (49% / 67%), Evidence first in about 19-35%. Goal is an algebraic recipe (P1, P2, C) or a plain-language template.\n- **Agree/Disagree (119):** speaker-named steps. \"Speaker's Claims > Speaker's Responses > Goal\", often a numbered claim list with \"Does [speaker 2] disagree?\" per claim.\n- **Method (91):** Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (37%) for one speaker; \"X's Conclusion > X's Evidence > Y's Response > Evaluate > Goal\" for two speakers.\n- **Evaluate (28):** Conclusion > Evidence > Evaluate > Goal (75%).\n\n## 6. Recurring phrasing conventions\n\n- **Frames:** \"Given that ... how could we (still) argue that ...\" (Weaken, Strengthen, NA, Flaw); \"Curious Fact ... Author's Explanation ... Alternate Explanation / Plausibility\" (any causal argument); \"Given that ... How can it be that ...\" (Paradox); \"If Evidence, then Conclusion\" (Principle, SA).\n- **Tests in choice notes:** negate it and ask if it weakens (NA); \"fails to consider X\" means ask whether X weakens, \"presumes X\" means ask whether X is necessary (Flaw); \"argues X by Y: X must match the conclusion and Y the evidence\" (Method, Flaw); a rule can only prove its right-hand side (Principle, SA); \"can we support the Agree position and the Disagree position?\" (Agree/Disagree); \"Why should we believe this?\" (Role, Main Conclusion).\n- **Recurring trap names:** Too Strong (the most common NA and MBT tag), Out of Scope, No Impact, Unclear Impact, No Distinction (Paradox), Deepens Paradox, Wrong Flaw / Not an Objection (Flaw), Bad Conclusion / Evidence / Trigger Match (Principle, Parallel), Premise / Last-Claim Trap / Opposing Position (Main Conclusion), Unsupported Agree/Disagree Position (Agree/Disagree), Fake Opposite / Illegal Negation (NA), Reversal (SA). Tags come from the local markdown; the dump does not include them.\n- **Rules stated as rules:** \"Most X can only be concluded from a Most X premise\"; \"some / sometimes / can is almost always wrong on Strengthen, Weaken, Paradox, SA\"; \"the second speaker almost never denies the first speaker's evidence\"; \"about 85-90% of Main Conclusion questions put the conclusion in the first sentence or after a pivot\"; \"on EXCEPT, three of the working answers usually work one way and one works another\".\n- **Voice habits that should not be copied:** mocking the question or answer (\"hot garbage\", \"so, so dumb\", \"unthinkably weird\", \"dumpster fire\"), and the PT157/158 em-dash register.\n\n## 7. `Explanations/targeted-questions/`\n\nThree files: a README and two explanations, PT134-S1-Q16 (Flaw, belief vs implication, answer A) and PT158-S4-Q24 (Weaken, food-supply chain, answer D). I've built the inventory, 80 candidates and a 50-item golden set, and did it read-only from the DB dump (PT101–PT159). I read about 125 explanations. The scores are my judgment from reading each one once, so treat 11 and 12 as a tie.

**What counts as "Standard".** The database has 236 explicit `standard` rows (126 of them in PT157/158) and 3,183 `single` rows. No question has both, and both have the same shape, so I used `standard` where it exists and `single` everywhere else.

**Totals per family** (explained / complete, meaning full breakdown plus five choice notes):

| Family | Explained | Complete |
|---|---|---|
| Flaw | 524 | 488 |
| Must Be True / Most Supported | 462 | 348 |
| Necessary Assumption | 352 | 325 |
| Weaken | 335 | 295 |
| Strengthen | 277 | 245 |
| Paradox | 213 | 195 |
| Sufficient Assumption | 193 | 180 |

| Main Conclusion | 144 | 99 |

| Agree/Disagree | 119 | 112 |
| Parallel | 100 | 97 |
| Principle-Conform | 99 | 85 |
| Method | 91 | 85 |
| Evaluate | 28 | 27 |

**Top pick per family:**
- **Must Be True:** PT145-S2-Q23. It refutes the "most" traps with worked counterexample numbers.
- **Flaw:** PT102-S2-Q9. It builds the "how could we argue the opposite?" objection before reading the choices.
- **Paradox:** PT151-S2-Q13. Its prediction is tied to what changed.
- **Necessary Assumption:** PT154-S1-Q18. It names two precise gaps and negates every choice.
- **Principle-Strengthen:** PT138-S3-Q1. It shows why a tradeoff principle with no "should" in it still justifies the conclusion.
- **Principle-Conform:** PT151-S2-Q4. It checks every answer's trigger and outcome against the stimulus.
- **Weaken:** PT155-S1-Q23. Its sentence-frame method for EXCEPT questions is the best one in the corpus.
- **Method:** PT133-S1-Q17. It teaches "argues X by Y": X must match the conclusion, Y the evidence.
- **Parallel:** PT108-S2-Q16. It gives both an algebraic and a plain-language model.
- **Parallel Flaw:** PT154-S2-Q10. It shows that the flaw is the tiny sample, not the personal experience.
- **Strengthen:** PT146-S2-Q13. It offers a second hypothetical correct answer.
- **Agree/Disagree:** PT150-S3-Q15. It names the exact point of friction and tests both speakers on every choice.
- **Main Conclusion:** PT139-S4-Q1. It replaces "that view" with the specific claim before matching.
- **Role:** PT119-S4-Q25. It uses "although" to predict a concession.
- **Sufficient Assumption:** PT146-S2-Q3. Clean missing link, with the contrapositive shown.
- **Evaluate:** PT141-S4-Q6. It tests each question by imagining the answers to it.

**How the rubric was built.** I compared 10 strong and 10 loose-but-complete explanations. Length doesn't separate them. What does:
- The strong Evaluate step argues with the argument instead of restating it.
- The strong Goal names the answer, not the task.
- Every wrong answer gets a reason and usually a test. Loose ones average one verdict-only note per question ("This is irrelevant").
- The most popular trap gets the most attention.
- The correct-answer note teaches the move, not just the key.

"Learner value" was the criterion that most often separated a 10 from a 12.
